questions.q: Why must perplexity be computed on a held-out validation split rather than the training data?
options: Validation data trains faster than training data
Measuring on training data would mostly reflect memorization rather than how well the model generalizes to text it never directly learned from
PyTorch's cross_entropy function requires two separate datasets to run
There is no actual difference between the two splits
questions.explain: A model can drive training loss down by memorizing training data without learning anything that transfers; a held-out validation split is the only way to measure genuine generalization.

questions.q: How is perplexity related to cross-entropy loss?
options: Perplexity equals the cross-entropy loss squared
Perplexity is exp(average cross-entropy loss per token) — exponentiating the loss gives a more intuitive 'effective number of choices' reading
Perplexity and cross-entropy loss are unrelated metrics
Perplexity is the cross-entropy loss divided by the vocabulary size
questions.explain: Perplexity is defined as exp(loss), converting the raw cross-entropy value into a number interpretable as roughly how many tokens the model is effectively choosing among at each step.

questions.q: In the evaluation loop, why use reduction="sum" and divide by the total token count, instead of averaging the loss per batch and then averaging those batch averages?
options: reduction="sum" runs faster on GPU
Summing total loss and total tokens across all batches before dividing weights every token equally, avoiding mis-weighting batches that happen to have fewer tokens
The default reduction mode causes a runtime error with validation data
It has no effect on the computed perplexity value
questions.explain: Averaging per-batch averages and then averaging those would implicitly give batches with fewer tokens disproportionate influence; summing total loss and total tokens first, then dividing once, weights every token in the dataset equally.

questions.q: Why are model.eval() and torch.no_grad() both used during perplexity evaluation?
options: model.eval() deletes the model's weights; torch.no_grad() reloads them
model.eval() disables dropout so evaluation reflects real learned behavior, and torch.no_grad() skips gradient tracking since no backward pass is needed, saving memory and time
Both are required only when using a GPU
They have no effect in PyTorch and are included only by convention
questions.explain: model.eval() turns off training-only behaviors like dropout, and torch.no_grad() tells autograd not to build a computation graph, which is unnecessary overhead when you're only computing a metric, not updating weights.

questions.q: Why can't perplexity alone guarantee that a model's free-running text generations are good?
options: Perplexity is always exactly 1 regardless of model quality

Perplexity is measured with teacher forcing — real previous tokens are always fed in — whereas real generation feeds the model's own previous outputs back in, where small errors can compound into repetition or incoherence
Perplexity can only be computed on images, not text
Perplexity measures training speed, not prediction quality
questions.explain: Teacher-forced evaluation always supplies the correct previous token, which differs from autoregressive generation where the model's own (possibly imperfect) output feeds back in — so a good perplexity score doesn't guarantee good free-running generations, and reading actual samples is still necessary.
